newsitem.title: UK: UK financial watchdog's new risk rating due soon.
newsitem.headline: UK financial watchdog's new risk rating due soon.

text.p: British financial watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) will next week release details of a new more in-depth risk-exposure rating system for firms it regulates.
"Next week SFA will be publishing further details about its approach to risk assessment that it initially notified the industry of last July," SFA spokesman David Jones told Reuters.

Concerns about how vulnerable a securities firm or investment bank is to market or counterparty risk were heightened by the collapse of Barings in February 1995 under multi-million pound derivatives losses.

This and other examples of losses going undetected have led to industry-wide attempts to improve how a firm's risk profile is assessed. There have also been moves to lessen the burden on firms which are less risky.
Jones said details of the new criteria for assessing the risk exposure of SFA-regulated firms would be announced in its "Briefing" magazine.
Later in the summer all SFA-regulated firms would be notified of the individual risk-exposure rating they had been assigned.
The SFA, one of three frontline regulators which report to Britain's Securities and Investments Board (SIB), said it was revamping its risk rating approach to firms last July.

This overhaul of the SFA's approach is based on five criteria and is driven by the principle that firms which have a greater risk exposure should have more frequent visits or greater attention from SFA inspectors than those which have a lower risk exposure.
The release of the new approach next week follows a year-long internal pilot of the scheme. The SFA has always had risk ratings but the new system is a refinement of the old ways of looking at risk.

If a broking or futures firm regulated by the SFA scores highly under the new regime, it does not necessarily indicate it is more "risky" than others but simply that it has a greater exposure to risk.
If a firm handles client money, rather than simply giving advice, then it would be classed in a higher risk exposure band and deserve more attention.
The five criteria will each be scored and the higher the overall score, the more attention the SFA will pay to a firm's activities, even if the company itself is not perceived as being high risk.
Assessment of firms' risk exposure will be based on five components.

These are the type of business a company is involved in and its funding strategy, the nature of its clients and whether it is responsible for safeguarding clients' assets, the firms it has as counterparties and therefore its credit risk, the financial health of the firm and lastly management competence.
This last element will concentrate on the type of management structure a firm has in place and whether it has the right controls and checks and balances.
Some commentators suggest that the ratings derived from the new approach should in fact be published as such information is likely to become public anyway.
But the SFA said it will make clear that the ratings should not be used by its firms as a means of gaining competitive advantage over others.
